extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians, AMS members, and historians of mathematics
extracted.subtask_short: AMS Notices article and submission guidelines
extracted.subtask_description: Page from Notices of the AMS containing a scholarly/history article on the development of mathematics (1875–1900) plus AMS publication/submission and production information (ERA-AMS, Notices submission scope, subscription/production notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: ERA-AMS publication standards
rubrics_metrics.description: ERA-AMS publishes high-quality research announcements of significant advances in all branches of mathematics. Authors may submit manuscripts to any editor. All papers are reviewed, and the entire Editorial Board must approve the acceptance of any paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ERA-AMS offers decreased turn-around time, fast access to specific areas, and up-to-the-minute research information. To obtain submission information and the template, send e-mail to era-info@ams.org with the word "help" in the subject line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notices submission scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notices Editorial Board encourages submission of articles on mathematics, the profession, and mathematics education, as well as shorter articles or reviews, and Letters to the Editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written material can be sent directly to the editors or to the Providence office (contact details on the page). This describes acceptable topics and formats for Notices contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial acceptance approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of papers for ERA-AMS requires review and approval by the entire Editorial Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formal gatekeeping requirement: papers are peer-reviewed and need collective editorial-board approval rather than single-editor sign-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic availability / e-MATH access
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of this publication is now available electronically through e-MATH on the World Wide Web (Notices One-MATH).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access instructions given (URLs, telnet access for non-WWW terminals) — signals expectation of electronic distribution and availability as part of AMS publication practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper permanence and durability standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper used in this Journal is acid-free and falls within the guidelines established to ensure permanence and durability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A production/material standard intended to ensure archival quality of the printed journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription and ordering requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscriptions and orders for AMS publications should be addressed to the American Mathematical Society ... All orders must be prepaid. A late charge of 10% of the subscription price will be imposed upon orders received from nonmembers after January 1 of the subscription year. Add for postage: surface delivery outside the United States and India - $15; in India - $34; expedited delivery to destinations in North America - $32; elsewhere - $67.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirements for acquiring the journal (payment, postage, late charges) and contact information for customer service are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational reform as driver of mathematical communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational reform is a kind of international common denominator relative to the formation of mathematical communities in individual national contexts between 1875 and 1900.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include reforms spurred by political unification, defeat in war, or philanthropy; the observation is a historiographical criterion for explaining the rise of national mathematical communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on pure research (Von Humboldt model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Von Humboldt's vision of higher education ... stressed the importance of pure research over utilitarian concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normative ideal (prioritizing research) is cited as a central factor in the professionalization and development of university mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic freedom (Lehr- und Lernfreiheit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insistence on academic freedom — the freedom to teach and to learn without political or religious interference — was a critical attribute in the development of research-oriented universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Academic freedom supported faculty research and training of independent thinkers; presented as a criterion for successful research institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and professionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition from laying the main emphasis on teaching to a dual activity in which teaching comprised only the lesser part of the remunerated activity marks the decisive step towards professionalization; in mathematics this produced increasing specialization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionalization is measured by research activity, specialization, and formation of a corps of students trained for research (requires both professors and students).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of internationalization of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Becoming an international mathematical community meant working together across political boundaries on common problems using shared techniques; formation of societies and journals, centennial celebrations, and cross-border training were indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: growth of national societies (LMS, AMS, DMV), journals, and the practice of scholars traveling abroad for advanced training; these are empirical markers for 'how we got where we are.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Deeper conceptual understanding (Calulus&Mathematica outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a comparative study: 'The C&M group obtained a higher level of conceptual understanding than did the standard group without much loss of [hand] computational proficiency.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion for assessing a calculus course: emphasis on conceptual gains as measured in controlled study; used to argue for pedagogical effectiveness of computer-based, student-centered courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain computational proficiency (balanced outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase in students' conceptual achievement without a serious decrease in computational achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful course should improve conceptual understanding while preserving computational skills — an explicit quality tradeoff to monitor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student engagement and positive disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The C&M group's disposition toward mathematics and the computer was far more positive than that of the standard group; labs were described as filled with engagement, enthusiasm, inquiry — 'the sound of thinking.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affective and behavioral indicators (engagement, enthusiasm, positive disposition) are treated as outcomes in evaluating pedagogical interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative learning and lab-style discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive side effect of the [computer] lab was the rapport that was established among the students ... When students gathered around the computer, worked together, and shared and developed ideas, a great deal of mathematics was learned. [Computer] capabilities helped students discover and test mathematical results in much the same way that a physics or chemistry student uses the laboratory to discover and test scientific laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricular design criterion: use of labs and collaborative tasks to promote peer interaction, discovery, and testing; explicit comparison to laboratory sciences as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of interactive graphics and open-ended/realistic problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Many problems involve interactive graphics chosen to drive home a mathematical idea ... provided the opportunities for the students to consider more open-ended questions and to encounter more realistic problems than often found in traditional calculus texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional design criterion: inclusion of interactive/visual tools and open-ended, realistic problems to deepen conceptual understanding and mirror research practice.
